Historical price study · data frozen 17 November 2026

If the RBI raises rates twice more, what does history say about Indian stocks?

History has no exact copy of today. The closest cases saw the Nifty go flat to slightly down over six months and higher over eighteen, with very wide gaps between cases. In this evidence, starting valuation and how many stocks joined the rally separated good outcomes from bad ones far more than the hikes themselves did.

This dashboard re-reads an existing descriptive study (35 comparisons, 26 index series, 2,467 stocks, 87 hikes) and adds new cuts, marked own analysis. Study results carry study. Nothing here is a forecast, a causal estimate or a recommendation.

Chapter 1

Where we stand: both central banks just turned from cutting to hiking

The RBI cut its repo rate to 5.25% in December 2025, then raised it to 5.50% on 7 October 2026. The US Fed did the same U-turn, cutting in December 2025 and hiking in September 2026. The trigger in India is inflation: annual CPI went from 0.25% in October 2025 to 6.09% in October 2026, the fastest twelve-month climb in the series that starts in 2014.

Where today sits inside a hiking cycle

Your scenario implies a three-hike, 75 bp cycle. One hike is done.

One hike of three is delivered, so the repo sits a third of the way from its 5.25% low to the assumed 6.00% peak. The study's own rule calls that an ongoing middle-cycle state (at least one hike delivered, 10% to 90% of the way to the peak). That rule is why it rejects January 2018, which came before that cycle's first hike.

Inflation: today's level has company, today's speed has none

Twelve-month change in India CPI, percentage points own analysis

Every inflation look-alike in this study matches the level of 6.09%. None of them arrived at that level after a 5.8-point jump in a year. The previous record (+5.6 points, January 2020) came just before the pandemic shock, so it says little about rate cycles.

Chapter 2

Your scenario, and why history cannot hand you one number for it

The scenario: repo 5.50% plus two 25 bp hikes = 6.00% by 17 May 2028, six quarters from now. Nobody specified which quarters the hikes land in, or what the Fed does. The study searched every month since April 2004 for the same setup and found zero exact matches.

The rate path the scenario allows

Each quarter the repo can sit anywhere in the shaded range; it must reach 6.00% by quarter six.

What "terminal" and "held" mean here

Terminal rate is the cycle's last hike. The study insists the historical match must reach its real cycle peak inside the 18 months. Without that rule, five dates from cycles that kept hiking later would count, and they show a Nifty median of +89.6%. The study keeps that number visible as a warning about convenient look-alikes.

Held at peak asks for the repo to stay at 6.00% until May 2028. No completed cycle did that after a two-hike finish. In 2018 the RBI cut again before the 18 months ran out.

Hindsight: every "what happened next to rates" filter uses information nobody had at the time. That is fine for describing history and useless as a trading signal.

Chapter 3

Four imperfect mirrors: a level twin, a shape twin and two contrasts

No date matches everything, so the useful move is to see which part of today each case matches. November 2022 matches today's rates and Indian inflation but sat late in its cycle with US inflation twice today's. October 2013 matches the cycle's shape exactly (one hike done, two 25 bp hikes left) but at rates two points higher. January 2018 started before the first hike at a rich valuation. August 2011 came at the very end of a long cycle.

Chapter 4

Do rate hikes sink Indian stocks? Across 87 hikes, mostly no

Look past the closest cases to every hike since 1994. After most groups of hikes, the Nifty's median result sits inside the normal range of any 6 or 18 months. RBI hikes land a little below the middle of that range, Fed hikes near it. The big losses cluster in specific cycles (2008, 2010–11) and vanish when you pool them.

Each comparison against a normal stretch of the market

Dot = median, bar = middle half of outcomes. Gray band = middle half of all monthly windows since 2004 for the same series. Hover for counts.

"Interior" hikes drop the first and last hike of each completed cycle. "Middle 10–90%" keeps hikes whose starting rate sat 10% to 90% of the way through the cycle's rise. Both labels need hindsight. n is the count of dates; dates from one cycle overlap.

Does the stage of the cycle matter?

Nifty median after hikes, grouped by how far the cycle had gone own analysis hindsight
After RBI hikesAfter Fed hikes

At six months, early-cycle hikes (the stage today sits in) had the strongest medians for both banks, and the RBI early group still leads at eighteen. RBI mid-cycle hikes were weakest, and most of those come from 2008 and 2010–11. Stage labels need the cycle's eventual peak, which nobody knows in real time.

When the RBI hiked soon after the Fed

RBI hikes within 45 days of a Fed hike versus all other RBI hikes own analysis

Today fits this pattern: the RBI hiked 20 days after the Fed. The nine "follow" hikes look far better, but they come from only two cycles (2005–06 and 2022–23), both of which saw strong markets for other reasons. Read this as a pattern worth watching, nothing firmer.

After stripping out the year's own trend

Initial study run, Nifty, 6 months study v1

The initial run compared each post-hike return with the median return from every month-start in the same calendar year. The gap shrinks to almost nothing for broad hike groups: hikes tended to land in years that were good or bad anyway.

Chapter 5

What mattered more than the hike: price paid, inflation's direction, the rest of the world

The study leaves valuations, earnings and global shocks unresolved. Using the same monthly dates and the local Nifty P/E history, a clear pattern shows up: the cheaper the market at the start, the better the next 18 months, whether or not hikes followed.

Starting valuation versus the next 18 months

Each dot is a monthly snapshot, July 2006 to May 2025. Horizontal ticks show the median for each valuation band. own analysis
RBI hikes followed within 18 monthsNo RBI hike followedBand medianToday's P/E range

Inflation level versus inflation direction

Nifty median 6 months after months with India CPI near 6.09% study

Matching the inflation level gives a healthy median. Adding the condition that inflation was still rising, which is true today, cuts the six-month median roughly in half. Narrower bands shrink the sample without making any forecast more precise.

The global piece no case matches

US annual CPI at each case's start versus today's 3.7%

November 2022 is the study's only ongoing-cycle case near today's Indian rates and inflation, but US inflation then was about 7.75%. Requiring both countries' inflation within a point of today leaves no ongoing-cycle case at all.

Chapter 6

Sectors and company size: the winners keep changing

Sector leadership flipped with the case and with the holding period. In November 2022, FMCG led at six months while Realty led at eighteen with +122%. In January 2018, Realty lost 19% over the same span. Across every RBI hike with sector data, FMCG beat the Nifty over six months after 82% of hikes, Auto after 79% and Bank after 70%. Media beat it after only 15%, and Realty and Energy after about a quarter.

Chapter 7

Beyond the index: the typical stock had a very different ride

An index can rise while most stocks fall. After January 2018 the Nifty gained 9.2% over 18 months, but the median surviving stock fell 41.7% and only 14% of stocks ended higher. After November 2022 the reverse happened: the Nifty gained 22%, the median stock 49%. If you own mid and small companies, the index numbers above understate both the risk and the upside.
